description: We are Team XOF a crew of full stack AI and software engineers passionate about orbital mechanics real time telemetry and space systems design. For the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge we built KAIROS a deterministic Lunar South Pole mission simulator and 360 degree NASA LOLA crater horizon raycaster that rescues delayed Artemis landings in 15 milliseconds. Our skills span TypeScript React physics modeling and UI design to turn complex NASA data into intuitive mission tools.
summary: KAIROS (Καιρός) is an interactive lunar mission-planning MVP developed by TeamXOF for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. As humanity prepares for sustained lunar exploration, a delayed landing opportunity could mean lost sunlight, reduced power availability and disrupted communication with Earth. KAIROS explores how these risks can be anticipated before they become mission-planning setbacks. By combining launch-delay simulation, 360° lunar horizon visualization, solar and Earth visibility assessments, and an Auto-Rescue optimizer that evaluates 600 alternative mission scenarios, KAIROS helps users identify more promising landing locations and touchdown windows when original plans change. Its mission is to make complex lunar landing constraints easier to understand, compare and act upon. Starting as a functional MVP, KAIROS lays the groundwork for future NASA-data-driven decision-support tools that could contribute to more resilient lunar exploration and sustained human operations on the Moon.
details:
KAIROS (Καιρός) — Lunar South Pole Mission Navigator

1. The Problem: When a Mission Delay Becomes a Lunar Survival Challenge

At the lunar South Pole, choosing where to land is only half the challenge. Choosing when to land can be equally critical.

Unlike locations near the lunar equator, polar regions experience extremely low solar angles. The Sun can skim just above the horizon, while nearby crater rims and elevated terrain can obstruct sunlight and communication with Earth. A change in the planned touchdown date can therefore change the conditions a lander encounters, potentially affecting power availability, communication opportunities and surface operations.

As humanity moves toward sustained lunar exploration, mission planners need better ways to understand these interconnected constraints and explore alternatives when launch schedules change.

2. Our Solution: Turning Mission Uncertainty into an Interactive Decision

KAIROS, named after the ancient Greek concept of the critical or opportune moment, is a browser-based lunar mission-planning MVP developed by TeamXOF for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

KAIROS demonstrates how landing-site conditions can be explored alongside mission timing instead of treating location and launch schedules as separate planning decisions.

Users can select from five representative lunar South Pole locations, adjust a launch-delay slider from 0 to 60 days, observe modeled changes in the positions of the Sun and Earth, and compare alternative touchdown scenarios.

The central idea is simple: when an original landing opportunity becomes less favourable, explore other locations and mission windows rather than relying on the original plan.

3. How KAIROS Works and Its Key Features

Launch-Delay Simulator: Users can adjust the planned touchdown schedule in six-hour increments. KAIROS recalculates its modeled environmental conditions as the date changes, showing how different delays may affect the selected landing location.

360° First-Person Lander Horizon: An interactive HTML5 Canvas visualization places users at a simulated lander viewpoint. It displays the modeled Sun and Earth positions against a procedural lunar horizon, helping users understand how local terrain obstructions can affect visibility.

Polar Radar and Site Comparison: A complementary polar radar view displays selected landing locations and their relative positions across the lunar South Pole. A comparison matrix allows users to examine multiple candidate sites under the same delayed mission scenario.

Solar Availability and Communication Assessment: KAIROS estimates solar availability using a configurable reference solar array and evaluates Earth line-of-sight clearance. These indicators illustrate how changing illumination and terrain visibility can influence potential power generation and direct-to-Earth communication.

144-Hour Surface-Stay Assessment: The prototype evaluates a modeled six-day surface mission using estimated illumination conditions and configurable battery-reserve assumptions, helping users explore potential operational constraints beyond the moment of touchdown.

600-Scenario Auto-Rescue Optimizer: When the original scenario becomes unfavourable, the recovery engine evaluates 600 combinations of five candidate locations and 120 alternative touchdown times across a 30-day window. It ranks promising alternatives using a preliminary feasibility score based on modeled illumination, Earth visibility and landing slope.

Voice Flight Director: A mission-control-inspired assistant generates Go, Caution and Abort briefings across POWER, COMM, GNC and CAPCOM stations. It supports browser-based voice playback and optional Google Gemini integration, with a deterministic fallback.

4. Benefits and Intended Mission Impact

The biggest benefit of KAIROS is its focus on mission adaptability.

A delayed lunar mission should not automatically mean abandoning an otherwise useful landing opportunity. Mission planners need to understand what has changed, which constraints have become more restrictive and whether another landing location or touchdown window offers better conditions.

KAIROS demonstrates a way to explore these questions through a unified visual interface.

Its potential benefits include:

  • Helping mission planners compare alternative touchdown times and candidate landing locations.
  • Making the relationship between lunar illumination, terrain obstruction and Earth visibility easier to understand.
  • Encouraging contingency planning by identifying alternative scenarios when the original mission timeline changes.
  • Making complex lunar environmental constraints accessible to students, educators and researchers.

Our long-term vision is to contribute toward more adaptable lunar mission planning, helping future exploration architectures investigate ways to reduce avoidable mission risks and make better use of limited operational windows.

5. Technology, Tools and Implementation

KAIROS was developed primarily with software-based technologies and does not require specialized hardware to run its current MVP.

Our technology stack includes:

  • React and TypeScript: Application architecture, interactive components and core calculations.
  • Vite: Development and application build environment.
  • Tailwind CSS: Interface styling and responsive mission-console layout.
  • HTML5 Canvas API: Custom 360° horizon and polar radar visualizations.
  • Vitest: Automated testing of calculation modules, optimization logic and user-interface workflows.
  • Google AI Studio (Gemini): Assistance with initial development scaffolding and visual assets, with optional Gemini 2.5 Flash integration for Flight Director briefings.
  • Web Speech API: Browser-native voice playback for mission briefings.
  • Git and GitHub: Source-code management and project collaboration.

The core application runs client-side in the browser, avoiding the need for a dedicated backend for its main calculations and visualizations.

6. Creativity and Innovation

What makes KAIROS different is the way it connects three traditionally separate mission-planning considerations: landing location, mission timing and operational conditions.

Rather than presenting users with static lunar maps or isolated environmental measurements, KAIROS creates an interactive mission-control experience.

Its most distinctive concept is the Launch-Slip Domino Effect: users introduce a simulated launch delay and explore how the same landing location may present different conditions at a different touchdown time. The Auto-Rescue engine extends this idea by screening alternative locations and times rather than simply reporting that the original scenario has become unfavourable.

The combination of a first-person lunar horizon, polar radar, mission comparison matrix, recovery optimizer and Flight Director briefing makes the underlying mission trade-offs easier to explore and communicate.

7. Factors Considered and Current Development Scope

During development, our team considered the extremely low solar elevations at lunar polar latitudes, local terrain obstruction, changing Earth visibility, touchdown timing, surface-stay duration, estimated power reserves and landing-site slope.

We also considered the need for a responsive interface, fast scenario comparisons and accessibility without specialized hardware or a permanent backend.

The current submission is a functional MVP and proof of concept. Its Sun and Earth positioning uses simplified analytical models, its local horizon profiles are procedurally generated rather than extracted from complete site-specific LOLA elevation models, and its solar-power and communication indicators use preliminary scenario assumptions rather than validated spacecraft engineering models.

These limitations define our next development priorities: integrating actual NASA lunar elevation datasets, improving astronomical calculations through validated ephemeris resources, and developing more realistic power and communications models.

Our vision is to evolve KAIROS from an interactive hackathon prototype into a scientifically validated lunar mission decision-support platform. We want to help explore a future where a change in mission timing does not automatically become a lost opportunity for lunar exploration.
